title: Numbers One to Ten
description: Count from one to ten the way Sanaa does — with the th kept in ثنين and ثلاثة — ask how much something costs, understand a price in riyals, and read out a phone number digit by digit.
approach: GPA Phase 2 — objects counted on screen, fingers and coins as the here-and-now. Numbers are drilled as a chant first, then pulled apart for prices and phone numbers.
unlock_condition: ≥9/12 on the listen-and-tap quiz and a phone number read aloud correctly
can_do: Ask how much something costs and understand the answer
Say a phone number digit by digit

grammar.title: بكم؟ and كم؟ — how much, how many
grammar.explanation: For a price, Yemen asks بكم — 'for how much': بكم الخبز؟ 'how much is the bread?'. The answer is a number plus ريال: بخمسة ريال 'for five riyals'. For counting things, كم on its own: كم جاهل عندك؟ 'how many kids do you have?' — and the thing counted stays singular after كم. The question word can start the sentence or end it; both are natural in Sanaa.

examples.english: How many teas do you want?

culture.title: Riyals, change and the first price
culture.note: Yemen's money is the ريال, and after any number the word stays singular: خمسة ريال, عشرة ريال. Coins have all but vanished, so small change means small notes, and a shopkeeper who has none will round in your favour or hand you a sweet. The first price you hear in a souq is an opening, not a verdict: ask بكم, look doubtful, and offer less with a smile — but in a bakery, a bus or a pharmacy the price is the price. Yemenis also count on their fingers starting from the little finger, and hold up the whole hand for five.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Feminine واحدة for ة-words: بنت واحدة. Comes after the noun, not before: شاهي واحد 'one tea'. Also 'someone': واحد من صنعاء 'a guy from Sanaa'.
vocabulary.image_scene: One single tea glass on a plain tray, large numeral 1 beside it.
vocabulary.video_hint: A vendor counting out items; واحد held up on a finger.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Sanaa keeps the th: thnayn, not the Aden or Egyptian itneen. Feminine ثنتين. Yemeni also has a 'two' ending on the noun itself — ريالين 'two riyals', شاهيين — which you will hear before you need to say it.
vocabulary.image_scene: Two tea glasses side by side on a tray, numeral 2 beside them.
vocabulary.video_hint: Two of anything being ordered or counted; the th audible.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Two th sounds in one word — the clearest place to hear that Sanaa keeps them (Aden says talaata). From three to ten the number comes before the thing: ثلاثة جهّال 'three children'.
vocabulary.image_scene: Three flatbreads stacked on a straw mat, numeral 3 beside them.
vocabulary.video_hint: Three items counted; parents saying how many children they have.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The ع in the middle is a squeeze in the throat between two a's — ar-ba-ʿa. Four is also the number of cups in a standard pot of qishr.
vocabulary.image_scene: Four small coffee cups arranged in a square on a brass tray, numeral 4.
vocabulary.video_hint: Four items counted; a price of four hundred (أربعمية) is also common.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Starts with خ. The open hand is five, and خمسة is also said to ward off the evil eye — a hand-shaped charm hangs in many shops.
vocabulary.image_scene: An open right hand, palm forward, fingers spread, numeral 5 beside it.
vocabulary.video_hint: A price of five or fifty quoted; a hand held up.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Doubled t — hold it. Same word across the Arab world; nothing to unlearn.
vocabulary.image_scene: Six eggs in a cardboard carton, numeral 6 beside it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Six items counted; ستة in a price or a phone number.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The ع is right after the b, so the word is sab-ʿa with the throat closing between the halves. Yemen's phone numbers start with 7, so this digit is heard constantly.
vocabulary.image_scene: Seven qat leaves fanned out on a cloth, numeral 7 beside them.

example.english: My number is seven seven three…

vocabulary.video_hint: A phone number read aloud; سبعة is the first digit in Yemen.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Four syllables and a th at the start: tha-maa-ni-ya. Often clipped to ثمان before a noun and when telling the time: الساعة ثمان 'eight o'clock'.
vocabulary.image_scene: Eight dates on a small plate, numeral 8 beside it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Eight in a price or a time; the clipped ثمان before الساعة.

vocabulary.teaching_note: tis-ʿa, the ع again before the final a. Yemeni's short i in the first syllable (not tas-) is the giveaway of a native speaker.
vocabulary.image_scene: Nine small keys hung on a wooden board, numeral 9 beside it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Nine in a price, a time or a phone number.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Starts with ع. Clipped to عشر before a noun and in times: الساعة عشر. Ten riyals is the smallest note you will handle.
vocabulary.image_scene: Both hands open, palms forward, all ten fingers spread, numeral 10 beside them.
vocabulary.video_hint: A ten-riyal price; both hands held up.

vocabulary.teaching_note: 'For how much' — the price question, with the بـ built in. Plain كم is 'how many' for counting. Point and say بكم ذا؟ and every vendor in Yemen understands you.
vocabulary.image_scene: A customer pointing at a pile of tomatoes with a questioning look at the vendor.
vocabulary.video_hint: Souq footage: a buyer asking a price; the vendor's number answer follows.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Sanaa word for money — the one that marks you as having learned Yemeni rather than textbook Arabic. فلوس is understood everywhere and is what the south says. Both appear in captions.
vocabulary.image_scene: A fan of Yemeni riyal banknotes held in a hand.
vocabulary.video_hint: Someone paying or counting notes; زلط / فلوس audible.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The unit of every price. Stays singular after a number (خمسة ريال) and takes the two-ending for two: ريالين. Also the name of the Saudi currency, which circulates in parts of Yemen — context says which.
vocabulary.image_scene: A single Yemeni banknote lying flat, the numeral large and clear.
vocabulary.video_hint: Any price quoted in a shop or market.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.english: Peace be upon you. How much is the bread?

dialogue.speaker: Baker
dialogue.english: And upon you peace. One is five riyals

dialogue.speaker: Baker
dialogue.english: Three… ten riyals and five. Here you are

sound_spotlight.explanation: The th of English 'think'. Sanaa keeps it where Aden, Cairo and much of the Gulf turn it into t or s — three of the ten numbers carry it, so counting is the drill.
Four numbers have ع before the final a. Say each slowly and let the throat close: ar-ba-ʿa, sab-ʿa, tis-ʿa, ʿa-sha-ra.
Before a noun and when telling time, the final -a of a number disappears in Sanaa: خمس ريال, الساعة عشر. Hear it now; use it in the time lesson.

lesson_sequence.detail: A bakery counter with breads stacked in threes. One line of English: you will count to ten and buy something.
Ten cards, one number each, with the objects counted on screen; audio plays as a chant, then one by one.
The three money cards (بكم، زلط، ريال) with illustration and audio; second pass with English.
Objects appear in a group; audio says a number; tap the matching group. Then reversed: see a group, tap the number you hear.
A vendor says a price; tap the right banknote combination. Trains بـ + number + ريال.
A phone number appears digit by digit; record yourself reading it; compare to the model. Feedback on ث and ع.
Counter rolls up. Nudge: count something around you to ten in Arabic tonight.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Count the stairs, the plates or the cars outside to ten in Sanaa Arabic — ث in ثنين and ثلاثة, ع in أربعة.
real_world_prompts.context: Shown on the lesson-complete screen. Here-and-now counting with real objects.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Next time you pay for anything, ask بكم؟ first even if you can see the price, and listen for the number.
real_world_prompts.context: Follow-up notification. Uses the price question in a real exchange.

real_world_prompts.prompt: Read your own phone number to your tutor digit by digit, then ask them to read theirs back to you.

video_needs.scene: A vendor quoting prices in riyals, a phone number being read out, children counting — the number said while the coins, notes or items are visible.
